meta.inspiration: A manager's year in a company with a problem: four quarters, a team, hidden facts that sponsors state wrongly, one market event and a plan for the year after.
meta.rights_note: Original scenario. The company, the people, the product and every number are invented.

company.name: Fieldledger
company.one_liner: Two merged software companies, a field-service app and an invoicing product, running on two stacks for the same customers.
company.market: India and the Gulf: service companies that send technicians to jobs and bill for them
company.business_model: A monthly subscription per account for the job app, and a fee on invoices run through the billing product.
company.product: Fieldnote, the technicians' scheduling and job app, and Ledgerly, the invoicing product, now sold together.
company.role: Tech lead for the merged platform. Your team is ten engineers, two designers and two analysts, from both companies.
company.brief: You report to the CTO. Fieldnote and Ledgerly merged a year ago and still run on separate stacks, with separate logins, release processes and data. Customers who use both are the happiest and the most irritated by the seams. The board wants one platform; the customers want nothing to break on the way. You have four quarters of twelve weeks.

stakeholders.name: Aditi Nambiar
stakeholders.says: The board wants one platform. I want one that nobody notices the move to. Tell me how fast we can go safely.

stakeholders.name: Rahul Pillai
stakeholders.says: A unified portal and automatic invoicing sell themselves. The seams are what customers complain about.

stakeholders.name: Mohan Das
stakeholders.says: The new platform will be slower for technicians in the field. Leave Fieldnote's sync exactly as it is.

stakeholders.name: Sheela George
stakeholders.says: Invoices must never change after the fact. Migrate nothing until the records are reconciled, and they are nearly clean.

stakeholders.name: Imtiaz Khan
stakeholders.says: Our biggest accounts use both products, and they are the ones who complain about two logins.

stakeholders.name: Jaya Reddy
stakeholders.says: Running two stacks costs us ₹1.2 crore a year. Retire the old one, and nobody uses its odd corners any more.

segments.name: Small service firms
segments.description: Cleaning, repair and installation firms with a handful of technicians.

segments.name: Mid-size service companies
segments.description: Companies with fifty to three hundred technicians and a back office.

segments.name: Facilities groups and enterprises
segments.description: Groups that run maintenance for hospitals, campuses and malls.

items.name: One sign-in across both products
items.about: A single account, single sign-on and one set of permissions for Fieldnote and Ledgerly.

items.name: A shared API gateway and contracts
items.about: One front door and one set of agreed contracts between the two stacks.

items.name: Migrate Ledgerly's data to the shared store
items.about: Move invoices, customers and history into one store, with a reconciliation run before each cutover.

items.name: Route invoicing through the new billing service
items.about: Send each customer's invoicing through the new service one cohort at a time, with the old one as a fallback.

items.name: A release train and freeze windows
items.about: One release calendar for both teams, and a freeze around customers' busiest weeks.

items.name: Shared tracing and dashboards
items.about: One view of both stacks in production. Raises measurement to level 2.

items.name: A compatibility shim for the old Fieldnote mobile app
items.about: Keep the old mobile app working against the new services while customers update.

items.name: Move everything to one platform in one go
items.about: Stop the line, rebuild on the new platform, and cut every customer over together. The CTO's favourite.

items.name: Retire the old Fieldnote web app
items.about: Switch off the old web app and move its users to the new portal.

items.name: Enterprise single sign-on and an audit trail
items.about: Directory sign-on and a record of who changed what, across both products.

items.name: Offline mode for technicians
items.about: Jobs, notes and photos that work with no signal and sync when it returns.

items.name: Automatic invoicing from completed jobs
items.about: Close a job in Fieldnote and the invoice appears in Ledgerly, priced and ready.

items.name: Shared test and build infrastructure
items.about: One build pipeline and one set of test environments for both teams.

items.name: Runbooks and an on-call rota for both stacks
items.about: Write down how each stack fails and who answers when it does.

hidden.label: Share of Ledgerly's records that migrate cleanly
hidden.description: Finance says the records are nearly clean. The figure comes from a sample of last year's invoices, not the whole history.

hidden.label: How tightly the two stacks are coupled, against what the plan assumes
hidden.description: The one-go plan was drawn from the architecture diagrams. The diagrams leave out the scripts and shared tables that grew up around them.

hidden.label: Share of customers who depend on the old app's quirks
hidden.description: The CFO assumes nobody uses the old web app's odd corners. Nobody has looked at who still does.

hidden.label: Share of customers who use both products and are hurt by the split
hidden.description: Customer success says the biggest accounts use both. The count comes from the accounts that complain.

events.name: A large customer's jobs and invoices disagree
events.signal: A large facilities group has escalated: their invoices and their job records disagree, and they have copied your chief executive.
events.body: Their jobs live in one system and their invoices in the other, and the two drifted apart during a migration test.

causes.label: The two systems' data has drifted apart
A bug in the new invoice run

directions.label: Freeze changes for them, reconcile the data and report back

events.name: The only person who knows the old sync code leaves
events.signal: The one engineer who understands the old Fieldnote sync module has resigned, and a bug that corrupts some jobs is stuck.
events.body: Nobody else can safely change the sync code, and the bug keeps corrupting jobs.

causes.label: One person held all the knowledge

directions.label: Pair two engineers on it now and write the module down
Freeze sync changes until someone is hired

events.name: An audit across both products
events.signal: An enterprise customer's auditors want evidence of access controls and data lineage across both products within a month.
events.body: Neither stack can show who changed what. A failed audit would pause renewals.

causes.label: No audit trail across the products

directions.label: Commit to an audit trail with dates and show the plan

plans.name: One platform in a year
plans.pitch: Commit to retiring the old stack and moving every customer.

plans.name: Two platforms with a bridge
plans.pitch: Keep both stacks and invest in a clean bridge between them.

plans.name: Keep both as they are
plans.pitch: Sell each product on its own and stop the merge work.

root.prompt: Which of these do you believe is the main thing holding the merged company back?

options.label: The two stacks do not share customer data
Releases collide between the two teams
The mobile app is not good enough
Customers are confused by two prices

measurement.label: Two sets of dashboards
measurement.shows: Arrivals, paying accounts, customers and the money, from two stacks that do not agree. Nothing in between.

measurement.label: Core events
measurement.shows: Also the first step and the share of customers lost each quarter.

measurement.label: The full funnel
measurement.shows: Also every step and every conversion rate, by segment.

quarters.title: Two stacks, one company
quarters.opening: {company} makes {hold_profit} a quarter and has {cash} in the bank. The two products run on two stacks, with two release processes and two sets of customers. Of every 100 small firms that start, {per100_small} end up paying. Your team has about {road} weeks of engineering this quarter.

quarters.title: First results
quarters.opening: Last quarter {shipped} shipped. Profit was {profit}, {delta} on the quarter before. {learned} {pleased}

quarters.title: The shock
quarters.opening: Last quarter {shipped} shipped and profit was {profit}. Something has changed outside the team. Read the signal below, say what you think is behind it and whether you checked, and decide how to answer.

quarters.title: The term sheet
quarters.opening: The board will back one of three plans for next year. Profit last quarter was {profit}. Where you stand: usability {U}, reliability {R}, technical debt {D}, engineering trust {trust_eng}, leadership trust {trust_lead}.

revised.why: Written as 35-65 before the first run. The first run put the mean at 65.5, so the range was revised to 45-70 after seeing results. The developer seat's weights reward delivery and stewardship, which a careful manager earns without investigating, and the case's big bets are gated.

min_gap.why: The default is 25. The first run showed 24.3 in this case, because the developer seat's weights give the evidence dimensions 30% of the score and the textbook manager does well on the rest. The threshold was lowered to 20 after seeing that.
